consensus.consensusInference: The dispersion has collapsed to near-unanimity, and NOAA's August 13 outlook made the record scenario its base case: a 69% chance the event exceeds every El Niño since 1950 on the relative index (RONI ≥ +2.5°C for OND 2026), alongside a greater-than-90% chance of a very strong peak. IRI's mid-July ensemble had 23 of 26 models very strong at OND with every model holding El Niño throughout — exceptional agreement. The debate has narrowed from 'does it join the Super club' to 'by how much does it break the record': ECMWF and CFSv2 point beyond +3°C on the standard scale, while the RONI lens — which nets out background warming, the more honest gauge NOAA now co-standardises — still clears +2.5°C at better-than-even odds. When the models agree this tightly and the official outlook favours a record, only the magnitude ceiling is open.

timeline.inference: Read the shape carefully: this is the probability that El Niño is present in each month, not its strength. It sits near-certain (98–99%) through autumn and winter 2026, then declines through spring–summer 2027 — that fall is the expected end-of-event decay, not a weakening now. El Niño peaks in NH winter and fades the following spring; the ensembles project weakening into spring 2027. Meanwhile the strength probability is at its ceiling (>90% very-strong). Both hold: near-certain to persist through the 2026–27 winter, very likely to peak very strong, and expected to decay through 2027.
